es.q: List and explain the step-by-step formation of bilirubin from red blood cell breakdown.
es.m:
- **Red blood cell breakdown:** Old red blood cells are destroyed by macrophages in the reticuloendothelial system, separating haemoglobin into globin and haem; globin is broken down into amino acids and haem is converted into biliverdin.
- **Unconjugated bilirubin formation:** Biliverdin is converted into unconjugated bilirubin by biliverdin reductase, which is fat-soluble, water-insoluble, and potentially neurotoxic in excessive unbound concentrations.

- Reference values may differ according to sex, age, race, altitude, socioeconomic changes, and study or reference populations.

es.q: Outline the complete pathway of bilirubin metabolism, from the breakdown of aging red blood cells to its final excretion products in stool and urine.
es.m: Bilirubin metabolism begins with aging red blood cells releasing heme. Heme is converted to biliverdin by heme oxygenase, then to unconjugated bilirubin by biliverdin reductase. Unconjugated bilirubin binds to albumin and is transported to the liver, where it is conjugated with glucuronic acid by UDP-glucuronosyltransferase. These bilirubin glucuronides are excreted in bile into the gut. In the gut, they are converted to urobilinogen, which is largely excreted as stercobilin in stool. Some urobilinogen is reabsorbed via enterohepatic circulation and excreted in urine.

ai.clinicalScope: Blood cell disorders (anemia, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia) in adult patients presenting to low‑resource hospitals in East Africa
ai.title: Blood Cell Disorders
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Blood cells carry oxygen, fight infection, and stop bleeding. When their numbers fall or are abnormal, patients can feel tired, get infections, or bleed, especially in settings where malaria, HIV, and nutrition problems are common.

sections.p: Blood cell disorders refer to quantitative or qualitative abnormalities of red cells, white cells, or platelets that impair oxygen delivery, immunity, or hemostasis.
b: Anemia affects ~30% of adults in sub‑Saharan Africa, driven by malaria, hookworm, and nutritional deficits.
Leukopenia is common in advanced HIV and after severe malaria.
Thrombocytopenia occurs in dengue, malaria, and drug‑induced immune reactions.
Combined cytopenias suggest marrow infiltration (e.g., leukemia) or aplastic processes.

sections.h: Causes and risk factors, most likely first
sections.p: Identify the most prevalent aetiologies in the local context before rare causes.
b: Anemia: malaria, hookworm, iron‑deficiency diet, sickle‑cell disease, HIV‑related marrow suppression.
Leukopenia: advanced HIV, severe malaria, tuberculosis, chemotherapy, aplastic anemia.
Thrombocytopenia: dengue, malaria, HIV, drug‑induced immune thrombocytopenia, sepsis‑associated DIC.
Combined cytopenias: acute leukemia, myelodysplastic syndrome, severe sepsis, nutritional pancytopenia.

sections.p: Each cell line has a distinct production pathway and destruction mechanism that can be disrupted.
b: Red cells: decreased production (iron deficiency, marrow suppression) or increased loss (hemolysis, bleeding).
White cells: marrow suppression or peripheral destruction (viral infection, immune‑mediated).
Platelets: reduced megakaryocyte output, peripheral consumption (DIC), or immune clearance.
Cytokine storms in severe malaria cause splenic sequestration of all cell lines.

sections.p: Symptoms reflect the cell type that is deficient and the speed of decline.
b: Anemia: fatigue, pallor, tachycardia, dyspnoea on exertion, splenomegaly in sickle‑cell disease.
Leukopenia: recurrent infections, oral thrush, weight loss, fever of unknown origin.
Thrombocytopenia: easy bruising, petechiae, mucosal bleeding, prolonged bleeding after minor cuts.
Mixed cytopenias: generalized weakness, fever, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly.

sections.h: Bedside: history and how to examine
sections.p: A focused history and physical can narrow the differential before labs.
b: Ask about recent malaria episodes, deworming, HIV status, medication use (e.g., antimalarials, antibiotics).
Dietary history for iron, folate, B12 intake.
Examine for pallor (conjunctiva, nail beds), scleral icterus, splenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, petechiae, and active bleeding.
Measure heart rate and respiratory rate; tachycardia may signal severe anemia.

sections.p: Separate primary marrow disorders from peripheral loss or destruction.
b: Anemia: iron deficiency vs. hemolysis vs. chronic disease vs. sickle‑cell disease.
Leukopenia: HIV‑related vs. drug‑induced vs. aplastic anemia vs. early leukemia.
Thrombocytopenia: dengue vs. immune thrombocytopenia vs. DIC vs. marrow failure.
Combined cytopenias: acute leukemia vs. severe sepsis vs. nutritional pancytopenia.

sections.h: Investigations and how to read them
sections.p: Use a stepwise approach; when a test is unavailable, rely on clinical clues.

t.b: Quantifies each cell line; hemoglobin <7 g/dL = severe anemia, WBC <4 ×10⁹/L = leukopenia, platelets <50 ×10⁹/L = thrombocytopenia.
Detects morphology (e.g., sickle cells, blasts, schistocytes).
Identifies Plasmodium falciparum infection causing anemia or thrombocytopenia.
Detects HIV infection, a common cause of leukopenia and thrombocytopenia.

t.a: Serum ferritin / iron studies (if lab available)

t.b: Indicated when blasts >20 % on smear or unexplained pancytopenia.

sections.p: Guides urgency of treatment and need for transfusion.
b: Severe anemia: hemoglobin <7 g/dL (or <5 g/dL in children) – consider transfusion.
Critical leukopenia: WBC <2 ×10⁹/L with fever – start broad‑spectrum antibiotics.
Life‑threatening thrombocytopenia: platelets <20 ×10⁹/L with active bleeding – platelet transfusion.
WHO malaria severity criteria (e.g., hemoglobin <5 g/dL, renal failure) dictate inpatient care.

sections.p: Co‑morbidities common in low‑resource settings can mask or worsen cytopenias.
b: Concurrent malaria and HIV can cause overlapping anemia and thrombocytopenia.
Pregnancy physiologically lowers hemoglobin; differentiate from true anemia.
Chronic kidney disease reduces erythropoietin, leading to normocytic anemia.
Herbal medicines may cause marrow suppression or immune thrombocytopenia.

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause first, then provide supportive care.
b: Anemia: treat malaria with ACT, give oral iron (ferrous sulfate) if iron deficiency, consider folate, transfuse packed red cells only when hemoglobin <7 g/dL or symptomatic.
Leukopenia: start ART for HIV, treat opportunistic infections, avoid neutropenic drugs, consider granulocyte‑colony stimulating factor only in severe neutropenia with infection.
Thrombocytopenia: manage dengue with careful fluid balance, give platelet transfusion if <20 ×10⁹/L with bleeding, stop offending drugs, consider IVIG for immune thrombocytopenia.
Combined cytopenias: refer for bone‑marrow evaluation; start empirical broad‑spectrum antibiotics if febrile neutropenia.

sections.p: Recognize when the situation is life‑threatening.
b: Hemoglobin <5 g/dL with cardiac failure – risk of sudden decompensation.
WBC >30 ×10⁹/L with circulating blasts – suspect acute leukemia, urgent referral.
Platelets <20 ×10⁹/L with intracranial bleed – immediate neuro‑imaging and transfusion.
Persistent fever >48 h in neutropenia (WBC <0.5 ×10⁹/L) – start empiric anti‑pseudomonal antibiotics.

sections.p: Pregnant women, children, and patients with sickle‑cell disease need tailored approaches.
b: Pregnancy: give iron, folate, and malaria prophylaxis; avoid teratogenic drugs.
Children: use weight‑based dosing for antimalarials and antibiotics; monitor growth.
Sickle‑cell disease: hydroxyurea is avoided in pregnancy; vaccinate against encapsulated organisms.
Elderly: screen for renal insufficiency before iron or erythropoietin therapy.

sections.p: Most cytopenias improve with treatment of the cause; prevention reduces recurrence.
b: Anemia: iron supplementation and deworming reduce prevalence by up to 40 % in endemic areas.
Leukopenia: early ART initiation improves white‑cell recovery.
Thrombocytopenia: vector control for dengue and malaria lowers incidence.
Schedule repeat FBC after 2–4 weeks of therapy to confirm response.

sections.p: Be aware of false‑normal or false‑abnormal values in low‑resource labs.
b: Hemoglobin measured by point‑of‑care devices may overestimate in severe dehydration.
Platelet clumping on smear can falsely lower automated counts.
Malaria RDTs may be negative in low‑parasite‑density infections; confirm with microscopy.
HIV rapid tests can give false‑negative results during the window period; repeat after 4 weeks if exposure suspected.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden collapse with pallor or chest pain – possible severe anemia or hemorrhage.
Fever >38 °C with neutrophil count <0.5 ×10⁹/L – febrile neutropenia.
Unexplained bruising or bleeding with platelets <20 ×10⁹/L – risk of intracranial bleed.
New onset confusion or seizures in a patient with severe anemia or thrombocytopenia.

faq.q: Why is malaria such a common cause of low platelets?
faq.a: Parasite‑induced immune activation and splenic sequestration destroy platelets, and dengue‑like viral mechanisms may coexist.

faq.q: Can iron supplements be given during an infection?
faq.a: Yes, unless there is active bacterial sepsis where excess iron could fuel pathogens; give after infection control.

faq.q: When is a bone‑marrow biopsy essential?
faq.a: When blasts >20 % on peripheral smear, unexplained pancytopenia, or lack of response to empirical therapy.

exam: A 28‑year‑old woman with HIV presents with fever, pallor, and platelets 30 ×10⁹/L. Which investigation will most directly guide immediate management? — Peripheral smear to look for malaria parasites and schistocytes; if positive, treat malaria first.
In a patient with hemoglobin 6 g/dL, tachycardia, and no overt bleeding, what is the next step? — Give packed red‑cell transfusion if symptomatic or cardiac failure, then treat underlying cause.

How does severe malaria cause anemia beyond hemolysis? — Sequestration of infected RBCs in spleen, bone‑marrow suppression, and dyserythropoiesis; therefore antimalarial therapy plus supportive care is required.

A febrile neutropenic patient (WBC 0.4 ×10⁹/L) is in a district hospital without G‑CSF. What is the safest initial management? — Start broad‑spectrum anti‑pseudomonal antibiotics promptly; monitor and refer if no improvement.

Why is platelet transfusion not routinely given for a dengue patient with platelets 45 ×10⁹/L and no bleeding? — Transfusion carries risk and does not improve outcome unless platelets <20 ×10⁹/L or active bleeding.

What feature on peripheral smear distinguishes iron‑deficiency anemia from thalassemia? — Microcytosis with hypochromia and target cells in thalassemia; iron deficiency shows anisopoikilocytosis without target cells.

A child with sickle‑cell disease presents with acute chest pain and a drop in hemoglobin. Which complication should be high on the list? — Acute vaso‑occlusive crisis with possible splenic sequestration; urgent transfusion may be needed.

When is it appropriate to start oral iron in a malaria‑positive patient with anemia? — After initiating antimalarial therapy and confirming iron‑deficiency (low ferritin) or when anemia persists beyond 2 weeks.

Explain why a normal hemoglobin measured by a handheld device might be misleading in a dehydrated patient. — Dehydration concentrates blood, falsely elevating hemoglobin; re‑hydrate and repeat measurement.
A patient on long‑term TMP‑SMX develops pancytopenia. What is the most likely mechanism? — Drug‑induced bone‑marrow suppression; stop the drug and provide supportive care.
